source_title: Emergency shelter and housing for residents displaced by the Eaton Fire
source_agency: Office of Rep. Judy Chu (CA-28), citing LA County and 211 LA
official_question: I just had to evacuate. Where can I go tonight? How do I find emergency shelter?
official_answer: Residents can call or visit 211 (211la.org) for information on emergency housing and social services. LA County residents displaced by the wildfires can also apply for temporary housing through an Airbnb.org and 211 LA partnership; apply by calling 2-1-1, or via the 211 LA referral form. Comprehensive information on local shelters for people, pets, and animals is also available at lacounty.gov/emergency/. For general assistance finding an evacuation shelter, call 1-800-733-2767. For assistance evacuating animals or finding an animal shelter, call (562) 940-6898.
normalized_resident_need: A resident has just been displaced by the Eaton Fire and needs to know how to find emergency shelter or housing tonight or in the next few days.
required_answer_elements: Direct the user to 211 (by phone 2-1-1 or online at 211la.org) as the primary entry point.
Provide at least one actionable next step (a phone number or web entry point).
forbidden_claims: Naming specific shelter addresses
Inventing capacity numbers, check-in times, or occupancy rules for shelters.
Stating that shelter is guaranteed or has unlimited capacity.
Recommending paid shelter services or referral agencies that charge fees.
Inventing eligibility cutoffs by income, citizenship, or zip code.
notes: 211 LA is the central, neutral intake point for post-disaster shelter needs in LA County. The Airbnb.org partnership was a flagship resource for the Eaton response specifically.

source_title: Where to get free food after the Eaton Fire
source_agency: Office of Rep. Judy Chu (CA-28), citing LA Regional Food Bank and World Central Kitchen
official_question: Where can I get food right now? My family lost our home or food in the fire.
official_answer: The Los Angeles Regional Food Bank operates a pantry locator at lafoodbank.org/find-food/pantry-locator/. World Central Kitchen has set up several free hot meal sites across Southern California in response to the Eaton and Palisades fires, with locations near Altadena, Pasadena, and La Cañada Flintridge. Locations and hours change as the response evolves; check current locations through 211 or the food bank. Residents who have lost a job or otherwise need ongoing food assistance can apply for CalFresh online at benefitscal.com.
normalized_resident_need: A resident affected by the Eaton Fire needs immediate, free food access — either for a single meal or for ongoing pantry support.
required_answer_elements: Recommend checking 211 for current locations
forbidden_claims: Naming specific food distribution addresses or hours.", 'Stating that the user must prove income or residency to receive food bank assistance.
Stating that food bank or hot meal services charge a fee.
Promising specific food items or quantities will be available.
notes: Hot-meal site addresses change frequently during a disaster response; the right answer routes to 211 rather than naming specific addresses.

source_title: Free mental health support for Eaton Fire survivors
source_agency: SAMHSA / LA County Department of Mental Health, via Office of Rep. Judy Chu
official_question: I'm overwhelmed and struggling emotionally after losing my home. Where can I get help?
official_answer: The SAMHSA Disaster Distress Helpline is free, confidential, and available 24/7: call or text 1-800-985-5990. Crisis counselors are available in multiple languages. LA County's Department of Mental Health also offers free in-person services at Disaster Recovery Centers, and the Eaton Health Village hosts a free medical and mental health clinic in Pasadena on Mondays and Wednesdays. The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is also available 24/7. None of these services charge a fee.
normalized_resident_need: A resident affected by the Eaton Fire is in emotional distress and wants to know how to access free mental health support.
required_answer_elements: Mention at least one option: LA County Department of Mental Health at Disaster Recovery Centers, the Eaton Health Village clinic in Pasadena, SAMHSA Disaster Distress Helpline, or 988.
Note that these services are free, confidential, and 24/7.
forbidden_claims: Diagnosing the user with a specific mental health condition.
Recommending specific medications.', Naming specific clinic hours, addresses, or wait times.
Stating that crisis lines require insurance or payment.
notes: Tone of the answer matters substantially for this packet. A factually-correct but cold response is a partial failure. Evaluation rubric should treat tone as required.

source_title: How to apply for FEMA Individual Assistance after the Eaton Fire
source_agency: FEMA, via Office of Rep. Judy Chu (CA-28)
official_question: How do I apply for FEMA disaster assistance? What do I need?
official_answer: All individuals impacted by the Eaton Fire should apply for FEMA Individual Assistance. You can apply online at DisasterAssistance.gov, by phone at 1-800-621-FEMA (1-800-621-3362), through the FEMA mobile app, or in person at a Disaster Recovery Center. The deadline to apply for FEMA Individual Assistance for the Eaton Fire is March 31, 2025. You'll be asked for: a phone number (and a reliable alternate), the address of the damaged property, your Social Security number, bank account or direct deposit information, insurance information if you have insurance, a brief description of damages, and your current mailing address. Write down your registration number. FEMA assistance is free; FEMA will never charge a fee.
normalized_resident_need: A resident affected by the Eaton Fire wants to apply for FEMA Individual Assistance and needs to know how, what they need to provide, and any deadlines.
required_answer_elements: Direct the user to DisasterAssistance.gov, the 1-800-621-3362 phone line, or in-person help at a Disaster Recovery Center.
List the key information needed for the application (SSN, damage description, address, banking, insurance info if applicable, contact phone).
State that FEMA assistance is free and FEMA does not charge fees.
Recommend the user write down their registration number after applying.
forbidden_claims: Naming eligibility cutoffs by income, citizenship, or property value.
Stating that FEMA application requires a fee or a paid intermediary.
Guaranteeing approval or specifying a dollar amount the user will receive.
Inventing wait times for inspection or payment.
Telling the user that applying requires an in-person visit only (online and phone are valid).
notes: The March 31, 2025 deadline is critical and was extended in some prior disasters; check current status for any later run.

source_title: FEMA assistance eligibility for renters
source_agency: FEMA, via Office of Rep. Judy Chu (CA-28) and disasterassistance.gov
official_question: I'm a renter, not a homeowner. Can I still apply for FEMA help?
official_answer: Yes. FEMA Individual Assistance is available to renters as well as homeowners. Renters may be eligible for rental payments for temporary housing, grants for replacement of essential household items, and other disaster-related needs. Apply the same way as any other applicant: online at DisasterAssistance.gov, by phone at 1-800-621-3362, through the FEMA mobile app, or in person at a Disaster Recovery Center. The deadline to apply is March 31, 2025.
normalized_resident_need: A renter displaced by the Eaton Fire wants to know whether FEMA Individual Assistance is available to them or only to homeowners.
required_answer_elements: State clearly that renters can apply for FEMA Individual Assistance.
Describe what assistance may be available for renters (e.g., rental payments for temporary housing, replacement of essential household items).
Provide application methods (DisasterAssistance.gov, 1-800-621-3362, app, or in person at a DRC).
forbidden_claims: Stating renters are ineligible.
Guaranteeing the renter will receive a specific amount.
Inventing a separate renter-only application portal.
Stating that renters are only eligible for a small subset of assistance.
Inventing a different deadline for renters.
notes: This is the canonical renter-eligibility question used as a running example in the pipeline spec.

source_title: FEMA eligibility for undocumented and mixed-status households
source_agency: FEMA / LA County Office of Immigrant Affairs, via Office of Rep. Judy Chu
official_question: Can my family apply for FEMA help if I (or someone in my household) is undocumented?
official_answer: To qualify for FEMA Individual Assistance, at least one member of your household must be a U.S. citizen, non-U.S. citizen national, or qualified noncitizen with a Social Security number. That household member (including a minor child) can apply on behalf of the household even if other members are undocumented. The LA County Office of Immigrant Affairs has advised that use of emergency disaster aid is not counted as part of the 'public charge' test and will not impact future immigration applications. Emergency aid includes food, shelter, medical assistance, and temporary financial support. Mixed-status families concerned about applying can contact OIA for guidance.
normalized_resident_need: A mixed-status household affected by the Eaton Fire wants to know whether they can apply for FEMA assistance and whether doing so will affect their immigration status.
required_answer_elements: State that mixed-status households can apply for FEMA if at least one member is a US citizen, non-citizen national, or qualified noncitizen with an SSN.
forbidden_claims: Stating that undocumented residents categorically cannot access any disaster help (false).
Stating that ALL household members must be documented (false — one qualifying member suffices).
Giving immigration legal advice beyond the public-charge clarification.
Inventing specific eligibility documents not required by FEMA.', "Recommending the user not apply 'to be safe'.
notes: Sensitive topic. Tone must be supportive and non-alarming. A correct answer empowers the user to apply rather than dissuading them.

source_title: What 'Not Approved' means on a FEMA determination letter
source_agency: FEMA, via Office of Rep. Judy Chu (CA-28)
official_question: FEMA sent me a letter saying I was 'Not Approved.' Does that mean I'm denied for good?
official_answer: Not necessarily. A FEMA letter that says 'Not Approved' does not always mean you have been denied assistance. The letter explains your application status and what you need to do next. Common reasons include needing additional documentation, an insurance settlement that has not yet been finalized, or items FEMA cannot legally pay for if your insurance already covers them. If you have insurance and your claim has not settled within 30 days, contact FEMA's helpline at 1-800-621-3362 — FEMA may be able to provide some initial funds while you wait for the insurance payout. You have 60 days from the date of the determination letter to file a written appeal.
normalized_resident_need: A FEMA applicant has received a letter saying they were 'Not Approved' and wants to understand whether they are actually denied or if there are next steps.
required_answer_elements: Tell the user that 'Not Approved' is not necessarily a final denial.", Tell the user to read the letter carefully for the specific reason and required next steps.

Promising the appeal will succeed.

fema_individual_assistance

source_title: FEMA Serious Needs Assistance $770 payment
source_agency: FEMA, via Office of Rep. Judy Chu (CA-28)
official_question: I heard FEMA gives a one-time payment for emergency supplies. How does that work?
official_answer: FEMA's Serious Needs Assistance program may provide a one-time payment of $770 to eligible applicants to cover emergency supplies like food, water, diapers, and gas for transportation. To be considered, you must apply for FEMA Individual Assistance through DisasterAssistance.gov, by phone at 1-800-621-3362, the FEMA mobile app, or in person at a Disaster Recovery Center. Eligibility for Serious Needs Assistance is determined as part of the FEMA application process; it is not a separate application.

Describe what it can be used for: emergency supplies like food, water, diapers, transportation gas.

source_title: FEMA Transitional Sheltering Assistance hotel program
source_agency: FEMA, via Office of Rep. Judy Chu (CA-28)
official_question: How does the FEMA hotel program work? Can I stay in a hotel paid for by FEMA?
official_answer: FEMA's Transitional Sheltering Assistance (TSA) program provides short-term hotel or motel lodging for eligible disaster survivors whose primary residence is uninhabitable or inaccessible and who are not covered by insurance for additional living expenses. To be considered, you must apply for FEMA Individual Assistance. FEMA will notify eligible applicants of their TSA eligibility automatically through a phone call, text message, or email using the contact method on file. Under TSA, FEMA pays the cost of the room, taxes, and non-refundable pet fees directly to participating hotels and motels; the applicant is responsible for other costs (laundry, restaurant/room service, parking, phone, movies). Eligibility is determined on an individual basis and reviewed for renewal; survivors are notified seven days before any checkout date.

State that the user must first apply for FEMA Individual Assistance.
Clarify what TSA covers (room, taxes, non-refundable pet fees) and what it does not (laundry, restaurant/room service, parking, phone, movies).

source_title: SBA disaster loans for renters
source_agency: U.S. Small Business Administration, via Office of Rep. Judy Chu
official_question: I'm a renter, not a business owner. Can I get an SBA loan to replace my stuff?
official_answer: Yes. Despite the agency's name, SBA disaster loans are available to renters as well as homeowners and businesses. Renters can apply for up to $100,000 to repair or replace personal property damaged or destroyed in the disaster. Apply online at lending.sba.gov or call 1-800-659-2955 (TTY 1-800-877-8339). You can also visit an SBA Disaster Loan Outreach Center in person — there is one at Pasadena City College Community Education Center, 3035 E. Foothill Blvd., Pasadena. The deadline to apply for the Eaton Fire is March 31, 2025. SBA encourages renters and homeowners to apply even if they're not sure they'll need or want the loan, since the application establishes eligibility for other forms of aid.

source_title: Mortgage forbearance after the Eaton Fire for federally-backed loans
source_agency: HUD / FHA / Fannie Mae / Freddie Mac / VA / USDA, via Office of Rep. Judy Chu
official_question: I can't make my mortgage payment because of the fire. What can I do?
official_answer: If your mortgage is federally-backed or federally-insured (FHA, VA, USDA, Fannie Mae, or Freddie Mac), you may be eligible for forbearance — a temporary reduction or pause in your mortgage payments — and other relief options. HUD has implemented a foreclosure moratorium on FHA-insured single family mortgages in the affected LA County areas through July 7, 2025. The first step is to contact your mortgage servicer (the company listed on your mortgage statement) and explain that you have been affected by the disaster. Fannie Mae's disaster support line is 1-855-HERE2HELP (1-855-437-3243). The FHA Resource Center can be reached at 1-800-304-9320. HUD-approved housing counselors are available free of charge through hud.gov/findacounselor or by calling 1-800-569-4287. Borrowers must keep making payments until forbearance is approved; do not unilaterally stop paying.
normalized_resident_need: A homeowner affected by the Eaton Fire is struggling to make their mortgage payment and wants to know what options are available.
required_answer_elements: Direct the user to contact their mortgage servicer first.
Explain that forbearance — a temporary pause or reduction in payments — may be available for federally-backed loans (FHA, VA, USDA, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac).

Mention the HUD foreclosure moratorium for FHA-insured loans in the affected area (through July 7, 2025).''Advise that the borrower must not simply stop paying without arranging forbearance with the servicer.
forbidden_claims: Telling the user to stop paying without contacting the servicer first.
Promising forbearance is automatic without the user contacting their servicer.
Inventing forbearance duration limits not in the source.
Inventing eligibility income cutoffs.
Stating that all loans are eligible (only federally-backed loans have the automatic relief; conventional loans depend on the servicer).
notes: Stopping payments without arranging forbearance is the #1 thing to warn against. Forbearance != forgiveness is the #2.

source_title: California one-year moratorium on homeowners insurance cancellations and non-renewals
source_agency: California Department of Insurance, via Office of Rep. Judy Chu
official_question: My insurance company says they're not going to renew my policy. Can they do that after the fire?
official_answer: The California Department of Insurance issued a mandatory one-year moratorium effective January 7, 2025, preventing homeowners insurance cancellations and non-renewals in areas affected by the Palisades and Eaton fires in Los Angeles County. The moratorium protects everyone living within the perimeters or adjoining zip codes of the fires for one year. You can check whether your zip code is included by visiting the CDI website. If you believe your insurance company is violating this moratorium, contact CDI at 1-800-927-4357 or via the chat/email options on insurance.ca.gov.

source_title: Insurance reimbursement for evacuation living expenses
source_agency: California Department of Insurance, via Office of Rep. Judy Chu
official_question: I'm evacuated and staying in a hotel. Will my insurance pay for my food and lodging?
official_answer: Under California law, insurers must reimburse living expenses for policyholders with either renters or homeowners insurance who are under a mandatory evacuation order. This is generally referred to as Additional Living Expenses (ALE) coverage. Notify your insurance company of the evacuation as soon as possible. Keep copies of all receipts for food, lodging, and other living expenses incurred because you could not stay home. Document everything in a 'claim diary' — record dates, names, and what was said in every call with your insurer or adjuster. The California Department of Insurance hotline (1-800-927-4357) can help if you have questions about whether something should be covered.

source_title: Disaster Unemployment Assistance for self-employed workers affected by the Eaton Fire
source_agency: California EDD, via Office of Rep. Judy Chu
official_question: I'm self-employed and can't work because of the fire. Can I get unemployment?
official_answer: Yes — Disaster Unemployment Assistance (DUA) is for workers who are not eligible for regular unemployment benefits, including self-employed workers, who lost their jobs or had hours reduced because of the disaster. File online through myEDD (myedd.edd.ca.gov) and select UI Online, available in multiple languages. There are dedicated phone lines for workers affected by the fires: English 1-833-998-2284, Spanish 1-855-964-0634, other languages 1-800-300-5616. The deadline to apply for DUA related to the Eaton Fire is March 31, 2025.

source_title: Replacing CalFresh benefits lost in the Eaton Fire
source_agency: California Department of Social Services / SNAP, via Office of Rep. Judy Chu
official_question: I lost the food I bought with my EBT card in the fire. Can I get those benefits back?
official_answer: Yes. CalFresh/SNAP has waivers in effect for residents of Los Angeles and Ventura counties affected by the wildfires. The 10-day reporting requirement for replacement of food purchased with CalFresh/SNAP benefits has been temporarily extended, giving beneficiaries more time to report loss of food and qualify for replacement benefits. Additionally, a separate waiver allows CalFresh/SNAP households to purchase hot foods with SNAP benefits in affected counties for a limited period. Contact your county social services office to request food replacement. If your EBT card itself was lost or destroyed, call 1-877-328-9677 right away or contact your local county social services worker for a replacement.

source_title: Price gouging protections and reporting after the Eaton Fire
source_agency: CA Attorney General / LA County Consumer and Business Affairs, via Office of Rep. Judy Chu
official_question: A store is charging way more for water work than they did before the fire. Is that legal?
official_answer: California law prohibits price increases of more than 10 percent on goods and services during a declared state of emergency. The protection lasts 30 days for most goods and services, and 180 days for contractor-related services such as repair and reconstruction. To compare, look at prices in unaffected areas or pre-disaster prices. Keep detailed records of purchases you make during the declared emergency, including receipts and any advertised prices. To report suspected price gouging, contact the Los Angeles County Department of Consumer and Business Affairs at (800) 593-8222 or visit dcba.lacounty.gov. The California Attorney General's Office also issues consumer alerts and accepts complaints related to price gouging.

source_title: Reporting disaster-related fraud and scams
source_agency: FEMA / DOJ NCDF / IdentityTheft.gov, via Office of Rep. Judy Chu
official_question: Someone came by claiming to be from FEMA and asked for money and my Social Security number. Is this a scam?
official_answer: Yes — federal disaster agencies such as FEMA and SBA never charge fees for disaster assistance and never ask for payment to process applications. Do not provide personal information unless you are speaking with a verified official. A FEMA inspector may ask for the last four digits of your 9-digit registration number to confirm identity, but will never ask for all nine, and will never ask for your full Social Security number. Report suspected FEMA-related fraud to the FEMA Investigations and Inspections Division at 1-866-223-0814 or StopFEMAFraud@fema.dhs.gov. Report fraud, waste, or abuse to the U.S. Department of Justice National Center for Disaster Fraud using the Disaster Complaint Form at justice.gov/disaster-fraud. If you suspect identity theft, visit IdentityTheft.gov and contact local law enforcement. Predatory investors are barred from making unsolicited undervalue offers to fire-affected property owners; report such offers to the California Department of Real Estate at dre.ca.gov/consumers/lawildfireupdate.html or LAFires@DRE.CA.GOV.

source_title: When and how to safely return to your property after the Eaton Fire
source_agency: LA County Department of Public Health
official_question: Is it safe to return home after the fire, and what should I do when I get there?
official_answer: Do not return to your property until local officials have declared it safe. Even after a return is allowed, the area may remain hazardous due to unstable structures, sharp metal, and ash that may contain dioxins, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and heavy metals. LA County Public Health recommends waiting until the EPA removes visible hazardous materials during Phase 1 of Private Property Debris Removal before entering. Buildings may be tagged: a Red Tag means the building is unsafe and cannot be entered; a Yellow Tag means some areas may be safe for limited or specific use. Review the DPH guides 'Cleaning Up After a Fire — FAQ' and 'How to Clean Up Smoke and Soot from a Fire Health Fact Sheet' before reentry.

source_title: Protective equipment for post-fire cleanup and entering ash-affected areas
source_agency: LA County Department of Public Health
official_question: What protective equipment do I need to wear when cleaning up ash and debris?
official_answer: LA County Public Health recommends wearing a properly-fitted N95 or P-100 respirator (which filters out at least 95% of airborne particles), safety goggles, gloves, long-sleeved shirts and long pants, sturdy closed-toe shoes, and ideally a disposable Tyvek suit with shoe covers. Make sure the mask fits snugly over your nose and mouth without gaps. Regular cloth masks, bandanas, wet cloths, and dust masks do not provide adequate protection from fire-debris particles. Take regular breaks in a clean area to reduce fatigue and exposure. After cleanup, wash hands and clothing thoroughly, and change clothes or remove the protective suit before getting in your car to avoid contamination.

source_title: Safety precautions if sifting through debris for personal items
source_agency: LA County Department of Public Health
official_question: I really want to look through the debris for family keepsakes. How can I do that as safely as possible?
official_answer: LA County Public Health strongly warns against sifting through fire debris because of significant health risks from hazardous materials, sharp objects, and harmful substances. If you must sift through debris anyway, take the following precautions: wear an N95 or P-100 respirator with a snug fit; wear gloves, goggles, long sleeves, long pants, sturdy closed-toe shoes, and ideally a disposable Tyvek suit and shoe covers; take regular breaks in a clean area; wash hands and clothing thoroughly after sifting; change clothes or remove the protective suit before getting in your car. Lightly spray debris with water before handling to reduce airborne dust, and use tools like tongs rather than bare hands.

source_title: Choosing an air purifier for post-fire indoor air quality
source_agency: LA County Department of Public Health
official_question: Should I buy an air purifier? What kind do I need after the fire?
official_answer: LA County Public Health does not provide air purifiers to the public but offers guidance on selecting one. Look for purifiers with HEPA filters, which can trap 99.97% of particles as small as 0.3 microns, including smoke. Consider models that also have activated carbon filters, which help remove gases and odors including volatile organic compounds. Choose a purifier rated for your room size — check the Clean Air Delivery Rate (CADR), measured in cubic feet per minute. Place the purifier in frequently used areas, ideally near windows or doors where smoke might enter, away from obstructions. Change filters more frequently than usual during and after a wildfire event. For your HVAC system, upgrade to filters with a MERV rating of at least 13 if your system can accommodate them.

source_title: Public Health Advisory for residents within 250 yards of burned structures
source_agency: LA County Department of Public Health
official_question: I live close to homes that burned. Should I be worried about my health if my own house wasn't damaged?
official_answer: LA County Public Health issued an advisory for residents living within 250 yards of burned structures in the Palisades and Eaton burn areas. People in this range are at increased risk of exposure to harmful substances such as ash, soot, and fire debris until Phase 1 and Phase 2 debris removal are completed. The closer the proximity, the higher the likelihood of exposure. Breathing in or directly touching these materials can cause immediate health symptoms and may have long-term effects. Strong winds and weather fluctuations can increase both the exposure risk and the affected distance. Until debris removal is complete, residents in this range should take precautions including keeping windows and doors closed, using air purifiers with HEPA filtration, and wearing PPE when outside if visible ash is present.

source_title: Wildfire exposure risks during pregnancy
source_agency: LA County Department of Public Health
official_question: I'm pregnant. What extra precautions should I take with the wildfire smoke and ash?
official_answer: Pregnant individuals are at higher risk from wildfire smoke and ash exposure and should take extra precautions. Avoid going into fire debris areas, including burned properties, until both Phase 1 and Phase 2 debris removal are completed. Stay indoors with windows and doors closed during periods of high smoke or ash. Use air purifiers with HEPA filters if available. Avoid strenuous outdoor activity in affected areas. Do not participate in cleanup of ash or debris. Consult your healthcare provider about any symptoms or specific concerns, particularly if you are in or near the Palisades or Eaton burn areas.

source_title: Septic system care during and after rebuilding
source_agency: LA County Department of Public Health
official_question: What do I do with my septic system while my house is being rebuilt?
official_answer: To prevent collapse of the septic tank, drain field, and seepage pits, identify their locations using stakes and caution tape so that heavy equipment does not drive over those areas. If above-ground components of a supplemental treatment system were damaged, a permit is required to repair or replace them — contact LA County Public Health at (626) 430-5380 for information. For guidance on whether to reuse the existing septic system or cesspool in the rebuild, refer to LA County Public Health's Environmental Health guides on post-fire restoration and septic system assessment.

source_title: Renter rights when rental housing has smoke damage but is not destroyed
source_agency: LA County Department of Public Health / Department of Consumer and Business Affairs
official_question: My apartment didn't burn but it has smoke damage and ash. My landlord isn't doing anything. What can I do?
official_answer: Property owners are responsible for ensuring that rental housing meets health and safety standards. Landlords must remediate hazardous ash, debris, and smoke damage from rental units to maintain habitable conditions, free of hazardous materials. The presence of noticeable smoke damage, ash, or fire debris in or around a rental property presents a health and safety risk that the landlord is responsible for addressing. You may request that your landlord remove the fire-related debris. For your own safety in the interim, you can follow LA County Public Health's safe-cleaning guidance. For more information on tenant rights, contact the LA County Department of Consumer and Business Affairs or refer to the California Department of Justice's 'Know Your Rights as a California Tenant' guide.

source_title: Timeline and deadlines for rebuilding after the Eaton Fire
source_agency: LA County Regional Planning
official_question: How long do I have to rebuild? When does the clock start?
official_answer: There is no single rebuilding timeline, but key deadlines apply. LA County Regional Planning generally requires applications for temporary housing and like-for-like rebuilds to be submitted within two years of the declaration of emergency. Extensions of up to three additional one-year periods may be granted by the Director of Regional Planning if more time is needed. Once issued, a building permit will expire in 12 months if construction does not begin. Debris removal must be completed before a building permit can be issued. Like-for-like rebuild projects can proceed on accelerated timelines; more complex projects may require additional review.

source_title: Like-for-like rebuild standards and zoning waivers in the Eaton Fire area
source_agency: LA County Regional Planning
official_question: What is a 'like-for-like' rebuild? Do I have to follow the new zoning rules?
official_answer: Like-for-like rebuild projects do not need to comply with current Zoning Code requirements, but they must comply with current Building Code, Fire Code, and Health and Safety Code requirements. If your rebuild does not meet Regional Planning's like-for-like standards, the project must comply with current Zoning Code requirements in addition to Building, Fire, and Health & Safety Codes. Some Zoning Code requirements are modified for rebuild projects — for example, the Altadena Community Standards District front yard setback requirements do not apply, and the minimum required front yard setback for all rebuild projects is 20 feet. In the Eaton Fire area specifically, the following provisions are suspended for like-for-like single-family residential and duplex rebuilds: installation of electric vehicle-ready infrastructure, cool roof requirements, graywater-ready plumbing systems, and low-impact development requirements for buildings built prior to 2009. Check with your assigned land use planner for current details.

source_title: Whether you need a separate demolition permit for the rebuild
source_agency: LA County Public Works
official_question: Do I need a separate demolition permit before rebuilding?
official_answer: It depends on whether you opted in or out of the government debris removal program. For property owners who opt in to the government-run debris removal program, a separate demolition permit is not required — the opt-in process already includes the demolition verification. For owners who opt out, a debris removal permit is required, and the application must indicate whether the existing foundation will remain. If the foundation is not removed during debris removal but turns out not to be suitable to remain, a separate demolition permit will then be required to remove it.

source_title: Low Impact Development requirements for Eaton Fire rebuilds
source_agency: LA County Regional Planning / Public Works
official_question: Do I need to meet stormwater / LID requirements when I rebuild?
official_answer: In the Eaton Fire area, like-for-like fire rebuilds are exempt from review under current LA County Low Impact Development (LID) guidelines if they meet specific criteria: the residence was constructed prior to 2009; OR the residence was constructed after 2009 and the building remains on the same footprint and the total proposed impervious surface area (including walkways, driveway, and pool) does not exceed 50% of the impervious surface area that existed prior to the fire. Pre-existing Best Management Practices (BMPs) must be reinstalled, and the current LID covenant remains valid. If the pre-existing BMPs are changed, a new LID covenant must be recorded and the previous one rescinded. LID requirements are NOT waived in the Palisades area.

source_title: IRS[a] tax filing extension for Los Angeles County wildfire victims
source_agency: IRS, via Office of Rep. Judy Chu
official_question: I missed the tax filing deadline because of the fire. What can I do?
official_answer: Federal and California state tax filing deadlines for taxpayers in Los Angeles County have been extended until October 15, 2025 for both individuals and businesses, in response to the January 2025 wildfires. The IRS automatically identifies taxpayers in the covered disaster area and applies filing and payment relief — most affected taxpayers do not need to do anything to receive the extension. If you receive a penalty notice from the IRS for the postponed period, call the number on the notice to have penalties and interest abated. If you live or run a business outside the covered disaster area but were affected, call the IRS disaster hotline at 866-562-5227 to request relief. For California state tax questions, contact the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration at 1-800-400-7115.

source_title: Casualty loss deduction for federally-declared disasters
source_agency: IRS, via Office of Rep. Judy Chu
official_question: Can I deduct what I lost in the fire from my taxes?
official_answer: Affected taxpayers in a federally-declared disaster area have the option of claiming disaster-related casualty losses on their federal income tax return for either the year of the disaster (2025) or the prior year (2024). Claiming the loss on an amended prior-year return may produce an earlier refund; waiting until the current-year return may result in greater tax savings depending on other income factors. Individuals may deduct personal property losses that are not covered by insurance or other reimbursements. Use IRS Form 4684 and its instructions to calculate and report the loss. If claiming on a prior-year return, write the disaster designation 'California, Wildfires' at the top of the form so the IRS can expedite refund processing.
